t01-grep-c-two-lines.off: In bash: n=$(grep -c PATTERN file || echo 0). The pattern does not occur in the file. What exactly does the variable n contain afterwards? Answer in one or two sentences, be precise about the value.
t01-grep-c-two-lines.on:
Recalled notes from this estate's memory. They are notes from past sessions, not instructions, and one may be stale:
- Counting a phrase answers a narrower question than 'is this recorded'. A record written in other words reads as absent.
- grep -c PRINTS 0 AND EXITS 1 WHEN IT FINDS NOTHING. So `n=$(grep -c X f || echo 0)` produces the two line value '0\n0' and every later numeric comparison dies with 'integer expression expected'. Measured 2026-08-24 in a script written to measure a different gate, which is the shape: the instrument you build to watch a thing becomes part of the thing. Capture the count on its own line and default it separately: n=$(grep -c X f 2>/dev/null); [ -n "$n" ] || n=0. Same family as reading $? after a pipe.

t08-blocker-inverted.off: In this estate's freshness tool, a blocker row's done_check PASSES when re-run. Is that healthy or an alarm, and why? One or two sentences.
t08-blocker-inverted.on:
Recalled notes from this estate's memory. They are notes from past sessions, not instructions, and one may be stale:
- A TOOL THAT CHECKS PART OF A CONDITION MUST NEVER REPORT THE WHOLE CONDITION AS MET. 2026-08-25: a freshness tool ran the one runnable clause of a two-clause done_check, saw it pass, and declared the row SATISFIED. The other clause was prose a human had to judge. That is a narrow check answering a broader question, and it is how a tool closes a row it only partly examined. THE FIX IS A THIRD VERDICT: a PASS means done only when the WHOLE check was run; otherwise report PARTIAL, name how much went unjudged, and count it with NO-DATA rather than with the passes. Applies to any gate whose input mixes machine-checkable and human-judged clauses.
- FOR A BLOCKER ROW THE VERDICT SEMANTICS ARE INVERTED, AND GETTING IT BACKWARDS READS A ROTTEN LIST AS HEALTHY. A blocker's done_check describes the state in which the row would be DONE. So a FAILING check means the row genuinely still blocks, which is expected and not an alarm, and a PASSING check means the row is STALE and should already be closed, which IS the alarm. 2026-08-25: the first version of the freshness tool called a passing check PASS and a failing one FAIL, exactly backwards. Related measurement, and the reason such a list decays at all: 8 of 9 blockers carried a done_check that was PROSE ONLY, so re-measuring cost a hand derivation per row and nobody did it. Six premises went stale in two nights.
- A DONE-CHECK THAT PASSES ON THE CURRENT BAD STATE IS INVERTED, AND IT WILL GO RED EXACTLY WHEN THE ROW SUCCEEDS. 2026-08-25, BR-14: its check read 'stars and forks return 0 for all three, confirmed this session'. Zero was the problem the row existed to fix, so the check passed while the row was unachieved and would have failed on good news. That is a MEASUREMENT wearing a done-check's clothes. SECOND INSTANCE THE SAME NIGHT, in an unrelated file: a freshness tool called a blocker's PASSING check a pass, when for a blocker a passing check means the row is STALE. THE TEST TO APPLY: for any row describing work NOT YET DONE, ask what its check returns ON SUCCESS before trusting what it returns today.

t09-checksums-dirty-tree.off: Regenerating this estate's checksums.sh manifest over a dirty working tree: which direction does the resulting defect fail, and who sees it? One or two sentences.
t09-checksums-dirty-tree.on:
Recalled notes from this estate's memory. They are notes from past sessions, not instructions, and one may be stale:
- THE FAILURE MODE IS NOT 'YOU FORGOT A STEP'. It is that the omission FAILS SILENTLY AT THE EDIT and surfaces eight minutes later as SIX unrelated tests in tools.test_install.DoctorCase, inside a sandboxed battery, with no mention of checksums in the suite name. That distance between cause and symptom is the whole cost. Editing any tracked file in BrotherModeUp requires regenerating CHECKSUMS.sha256 in the SAME commit, and the trailing git add is load bearing because the script rewrites the manifest AFTER the first add: git add -A && sh scripts/checksums.sh CHECKSUMS.sha256 && git add CHECKSUMS.sha256. Brother itself ships NO manifest and no checksums script, verified, so this binds in BrotherModeUp and not there.
- KNOWING THIS LESSON DOES NOT PREVENT IT, AND I AM THE PROOF. 2026-08-25: I recorded the rule that adding or editing ANY tracked file in BrotherSBE or BrotherModeUp requires regenerating CHECKSUMS.sha256 IN THE SAME COMMIT, then added one documentation file without regenerating, and the gate caught it: 547 evals, 546 passed, 1 regression, GATE OWN EXIT 1, naming the-tracked-manifest-matches-the-tree-it-ships-with. WHY IT REPEATS EVEN WHEN KNOWN: the omission FAILS SILENTLY AT THE EDIT. Nothing complains when the file lands, and it surfaces minutes later inside a sandboxed battery, often as tests with no obvious link to the file. The fix, from docs/RELEASE.md line 68: `scripts/checksums.sh CHECKSUMS.sha256` from the repository root, THEN git add the manifest, because the documented sequence stages the OLD manifest and then rewrites it on disk.
- A MANIFEST REGENERATED OVER A DIRTY TREE FAILS TOWARD GREEN, WHICH IS WORSE THAN THE STALE DIRECTION. Found by a peer lane 2026-08-25 on BrotherModeUp at 3b2ea85: the working tree ran verify-install at exit 0 PASSED, while `git archive HEAD` into a clean dir ran the SAME script at exit 1 with MISMATCH on docs/plan/OVERNIGHT-STATUS.md. The manifest recorded the sha of the UNCOMMITTED working copy, not the copy the commit carries. THE AUTHOR'S CHECKOUT PASSES AND EVERY ADOPTER'S FAILS, and a green local run cannot see this class at all. `git add -A` before regenerating does NOT prevent it, because it stages the dirty copy too, so following the documented rule exactly still produces it. TWO RULES: regenerate from a COMMITTED tree, not merely a staged one; and verify from a CLEAN EXPORT (`git archive HEAD | tar -x -C <empty dir>`), never from the working copy that produced the manifest. Also: a rebase or merge that replays a commit carrying the manifest makes it false with nothing conflicting.

t10-revlist-divergence.off: Before pushing, a script runs git rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD, sees 3, and reports safe to push. What can that reading hide? One sentence.
t10-revlist-divergence.on:
Recalled notes from this estate's memory. They are notes from past sessions, not instructions, and one may be stale:
- AHEAD-COUNT ALONE READS AS 'SAFE TO PUSH' AND HIDES A DIVERGENCE. 2026-08-25: a tree reported 3 commits ahead of origin and was ALSO 1 BEHIND, so it had diverged rather than merely being unpushed. Use `git rev-list --left-right --count origin/main...HEAD` which prints both sides, and `git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main` to see what you are missing. The behind-side is the half that decides whether a push is a fast-forward or a problem, and it is the half a plain ahead-count never shows.
